sentences.en: I think I was supposed to talk about my new book, which is called "Blink," and it's about snap judgments and first impressions.
And it comes out in January, and I hope you all buy it in triplicate.
(Laughter) But I was thinking about this, and I realized that although my new book makes me happy, and I think would make my mother happy, it's not really about happiness.
So I decided instead, I would talk about someone who I think has done as much to make Americans happy as perhaps anyone over the last 20 years, a man who is a great personal hero of mine:
someone by the name of Howard Moskowitz, who is most famous for reinventing spaghetti sauce.
Howard's about this high, and he's round, and he's in his 60s, and he has big huge glasses and thinning gray hair, and he has a kind of wonderful exuberance and vitality,
and he has a parrot, and he loves the opera, and he's a great aficionado of medieval history.
And by profession, he's a psychophysicist.
Now, I should tell you that I have no idea what psychophysics is, although at some point in my life, I dated a girl for two years who was getting her doctorate in psychophysics.
Which should tell you something about that relationship.
(Laughter) As far as I know, psychophysics is about measuring things.
And Howard is very interested in measuring things.
And he graduated with his doctorate from Harvard, and he set up a little consulting shop in White Plains, New York.
And one of his first clients was Pepsi. This is many years ago, back in the early 70s.
And Pepsi came to Howard and they said, "You know, there's this new thing called aspartame, and we would like to make Diet Pepsi.
We'd like you to figure out how much aspartame we should put in each can of Diet Pepsi in order to have the perfect drink."
Now that sounds like an incredibly straightforward question to answer, and that's what Howard thought.
Because Pepsi told him, "We're working with a band between eight and 12 percent.
Anything below eight percent sweetness is not sweet enough; anything above 12 percent sweetness is too sweet.
We want to know: what's the sweet spot between 8 and 12?"
Now, if I gave you this problem to do, you would all say, it's very simple.

What we do is you make up a big experimental batch of Pepsi, at every degree of sweetness -- eight percent, 8.1, 8.2, 8.3, all the way up to 12 -- and we try this out with thousands of people, and we plot the results on a curve,
and we take the most popular concentration, right?
Really simple. Howard does the experiment, and he gets the data back, and he plots it on a curve, and all of a sudden he realizes it's not a nice bell curve.
In fact, the data doesn't make any sense.
It's a mess. It's all over the place. Now, most people in that business, in the world of testing food and such, are not dismayed when the data comes back a mess.
sentences.zh: 真是一团糟。到处都是。现在，从事食品检测等行业的大多数人在收到混乱的数据时并不感到沮丧。

sentences.en: They think, "Well, you know, figuring out what people think about cola's not that easy."
sentences.zh: 他们认为，“好吧，你知道，弄清楚人们对可乐的看法并不那么容易。”

sentences.en: "You know, maybe we made an error somewhere along the way."
sentences.zh: “你知道，也许我们一路上犯了一个错误。”

sentences.en: "You know, let's just make an educated guess," and they simply point and they go for 10 percent, right in the middle.
sentences.zh: “你知道，让我们做一个有根据的猜测”，他们只是简单地指出，然后他们就选择了 10%，就在中间。

sentences.en: Howard is not so easily placated. Howard is a man of a certain degree of intellectual standards.
sentences.zh: 霍华德可没那么容易安抚。霍华德是一个具有一定智力水平的人。

sentences.en: And this was not good enough for him, and this question bedeviled him for years.
sentences.zh: 这对他来说还不够好，这个问题困扰了他很多年。

sentences.en: And he would think it through and say, "What was wrong?
sentences.zh: 他会仔细思考并说：“出了什么问题？

sentences.en: Why could we not make sense of this experiment with Diet Pepsi?"
sentences.zh: 为什么我们无法理解这个关于健怡百事可乐的实验？”

sentences.en: And one day, he was sitting in a diner in White Plains, about to go trying to dream up some work for Nescafé.
sentences.zh: 有一天，他坐在怀特普莱恩斯的一家小餐馆里，正准备去尝试为雀巢咖啡设计一些工作。

sentences.en: And suddenly, like a bolt of lightning, the answer came to him.
sentences.zh: 突然间，答案像一道闪电出现在他的脑海中。

sentences.en: And that is, that when they analyzed the Diet Pepsi data, they were asking the wrong question.
sentences.zh: 也就是说，当他们分析低怡百事可乐的数据时，他们提出了错误的问题。

sentences.en: They were looking for the perfect Pepsi, and they should have been looking for the perfect Pepsis.
sentences.zh: 他们正在寻找完美的百事可乐，他们也应该一直在寻找完美的百事可乐。

sentences.en: Trust me. This was an enormous revelation.
sentences.zh: 相信我。这是一个巨大的启示。

sentences.en: This was one of the most brilliant breakthroughs in all of food science.
sentences.zh: 这是整个食品科学领域最辉煌的突破之一。

sentences.en: Howard immediately went on the road, and he would go to conferences around the country, and he would stand up and say, "You had been looking for the perfect Pepsi.
sentences.zh: 霍华德立即上路，他会去全国各地参加会议，他会站起来说：“你一直在寻找完美的百事可乐。

sentences.en: You're wrong. You should be looking for the perfect Pepsis."
sentences.zh: 你错了。你应该寻找完美的百事可乐。”

sentences.en: And people would look at him blankly and say, "What are you talking about? Craziness."
sentences.zh: 人们会茫然地看着他，说：“你在说什么？疯狂。”

sentences.en: And they would say, "Move! Next!" Tried to get business, nobody would hire him -- he was obsessed, though, and he talked about it and talked about it.
sentences.zh: 他们会说：“移动！下一个！”试图争取生意，但没有人会雇用他——尽管如此，他对此很着迷，而且他一直在谈论它。

sentences.en: Howard loves the Yiddish expression "To a worm in horseradish, the world is horseradish."
sentences.zh: 霍华德喜欢意第绪语的表达方式“对于辣根中的蠕虫来说，世界就是辣根”。

sentences.en: This was his horseradish. (Laughter) He was obsessed with it!
sentences.zh: 这是他的辣根。 （笑声）他对此很着迷！

sentences.en: And finally, he had a breakthrough. Vlasic Pickles came to him, and they said, "Doctor Moskowitz, we want to make the perfect pickle."
sentences.zh: 终于，他有了突破。弗拉西克泡菜来找他，他们说：“莫斯科维茨医生，我们想做完美的泡菜。”

sentences.en: And he said, "There is no perfect pickle; there are only perfect pickles."
sentences.zh: 他说：“没有完美的泡菜，只有完美的泡菜。”

sentences.en: And he came back to them and he said, "You don't just need to improve your regular; you need to create zesty."
sentences.zh: 他回到他们身边说：“你不仅需要提高你的常规；你需要创造热情。”

sentences.en: And that's where we got zesty pickles. Then the next person came to him: Campbell's Soup.
sentences.zh: 这就是我们吃辣泡菜的地方。然后下一个人向他走来：金宝汤。

sentences.en: And this was even more important. In fact, Campbell's Soup is where Howard made his reputation.
sentences.zh: 这更重要。事实上，金宝汤是霍华德成名的地方。

sentences.en: Campbell's made Prego, and Prego, in the early 80s, was struggling next to Ragù, which was the dominant spaghetti sauce of the 70s and 80s.
sentences.zh: Campbell’s 制作了 Prego，而 Prego 在 80 年代初与 Ragù 相比，在 70 年代和 80 年代占主导地位的意大利面酱中举步维艰。

sentences.en: In the industry -- I don't know whether you care about this, or how much time I have to go into this.
sentences.zh: 在这个行业——我不知道你是否关心这个，也不知道我需要花多少时间来研究这个。

sentences.en: But it was, technically speaking -- this is an aside -- Prego is a better tomato sauce than Ragù.
sentences.zh: 但从技术上来说——这是一个旁白——Prego 是比 Ragù 更好的番茄酱。

sentences.en: The quality of the tomato paste is much better; the spice mix is far superior; it adheres to the pasta in a much more pleasing way.
sentences.zh: 番茄酱的品质要好很多；香料的混合要优越得多；它以一种更令人愉悦的方式粘附在面食上。

sentences.en: In fact, they would do the famous bowl test back in the 70s with Ragù and Prego.
sentences.zh: 事实上，早在 70 年代，他们就用 Ragù 和 Prego 进行了著名的碗测试。

sentences.en: You'd have a plate of spaghetti, and you would pour it on, right?
sentences.zh: 你有一盘意大利面，你会把它倒在上面，对吗？

sentences.en: And the Ragù would all go to the bottom, and the Prego would sit on top.
sentences.zh: Ragù 会全部落到底部，而 Prego 会坐在顶部。

sentences.en: That's called "adherence." And, anyway, despite the fact that they were far superior in adherence, and the quality of their tomato paste, Prego was struggling.
sentences.zh: 这就是所谓的“坚持”。而且，无论如何，尽管他们在坚持性和番茄酱的质量方面远胜出众，但普雷戈仍在苦苦挣扎。

sentences.en: So they came to Howard, and they said, fix us.
sentences.zh: 所以他们来找霍华德，他们说，修复我们。

sentences.en: And Howard looked at their product line, and he said, what you have is a dead tomato society.
sentences.zh: 霍华德看了他们的产品线，他说，你所拥有的是一个死番茄社会。

sentences.en: So he said, this is what I want to do. And he got together with the Campbell's soup kitchen, and he made 45 varieties of spaghetti sauce.
sentences.zh: 所以他说，这就是我想做的。他与金宝汤厨房合作，制作了 45 种意大利面酱。

sentences.en: And he varied them according to every conceivable way that you can vary tomato sauce: by sweetness, by level of garlic, by tomatoey-ness, by tartness, by sourness, by visible solids -- my favorite term in the spaghetti sauce business.
sentences.zh: 他根据番茄酱的每一种可以想象的方式来改变它们：根据甜度，根据大蒜的含量，根据番茄的味道，根据酸味，根据酸味，根据可见的固体——我在意大利面酱行业最喜欢的术语。

sentences.en: (Laughter) Every conceivable way you can vary spaghetti sauce, he varied spaghetti sauce.
sentences.zh: （笑声）无论你能想到什么方式来改变意大利面酱，他都改变了意大利面酱。

sentences.en: And then he took this whole raft of 45 spaghetti sauces, and he went on the road.
sentences.zh: 然后他带着这整筏 45 份意大利面酱上路了。

sentences.en: He went to New York, to Chicago, he went to Jacksonville, to Los Angeles.
sentences.zh: 他去了纽约、芝加哥、杰克逊维尔、洛杉矶。

sentences.en: And he brought in people by the truckload into big halls.
sentences.zh: 他把一卡车的人带进大厅。

sentences.en: And he sat them down for two hours, and over the course of that two hours, he gave them ten bowls.
sentences.zh: 他让他们坐下两个小时，在这两个小时里，他给了他们十碗。

sentences.en: Ten small bowls of pasta, with a different spaghetti sauce on each one.
sentences.zh: 十小碗意大利面，每碗都有不同的意大利面酱。

sentences.en: And after they ate each bowl, they had to rate, from 0 to 100, how good they thought the spaghetti sauce was.
sentences.zh: 他们吃完每一碗后，必须从 0 到 100 评价意大利面酱的好坏。

sentences.en: At the end of that process, after doing it for months and months, he had a mountain of data about how the American people feel about spaghetti sauce.
sentences.zh: 在这个过程结束时，经过几个月的努力，他获得了大量关于美国人民对意大利面酱的感受的数据。

sentences.en: And then he analyzed the data. Did he look for the most popular variety of spaghetti sauce?
sentences.zh: 然后他分析了数据。他是否在寻找最受欢迎的意大利面酱品种？

sentences.en: No! Howard doesn't believe that there is such a thing.
sentences.zh: 不！霍华德不相信有这种事。

sentences.en: Instead, he looked at the data, and he said, let's see if we can group all these different data points into clusters.
sentences.zh: 相反，他查看了数据，然后说，让我们看看是否可以将所有这些不同的数据点分组为集群。

sentences.en: Let's see if they congregate around certain ideas.
sentences.zh: 让我们看看他们是否聚集在某些想法上。

sentences.en: And sure enough, if you sit down, and you analyze all this data on spaghetti sauce, you realize that all Americans fall into one of three groups.
sentences.zh: 果然，如果您坐下来分析有关意大利面酱的所有数据，您会发现所有美国人都属于以下三组之一。

sentences.en: There are people who like their spaghetti sauce plain; there are people who like their spaghetti sauce spicy; and there are people who like it extra chunky.
sentences.zh: 有些人喜欢原味的意大利面酱；有些人喜欢吃普通的意大利面酱。有人喜欢吃辣的意大利面酱；有些人喜欢特别厚实的。

sentences.en: And of those three facts, the third one was the most significant, because at the time, in the early 1980s, if you went to a supermarket, you would not find extra-chunky spaghetti sauce.
sentences.zh: 在这三个事实中，第三个是最重要的，因为在 20 世纪 80 年代初，如果你去超市，你不会找到特别厚的意大利面酱。

sentences.en: And Prego turned to Howard, and they said, "You're telling me that one third of Americans crave extra-chunky spaghetti sauce and yet no one is servicing their needs?"
sentences.zh: 普雷戈转向霍华德，他们说：“你是在告诉我，三分之一的美国人渴望超厚的意大利面酱，但没有人满足他们的需求？”

sentences.en: And he said "Yes!" (Laughter) And Prego then went back, and completely reformulated their spaghetti sauce, and came out with a line of extra chunky that immediately and completely took over the spaghetti sauce business in this country.
sentences.zh: 他说：“是的！” （笑声） 然后 Prego 回去，完全重新配制了他们的意大利面酱，并推出了一系列额外厚实的产品，立即完全接管了这个国家的意大利面酱业务。

sentences.en: And over the next 10 years, they made 600 million dollars off their line of extra-chunky sauces.
sentences.zh: 在接下来的 10 年里，他们从特厚酱料系列中赚了 6 亿美元。

sentences.en: Everyone else in the industry looked at what Howard had done, and they said, "Oh my god! We've been thinking all wrong!"
sentences.zh: 业内的其他人看着霍华德所做的事情，他们说：“天哪！我们一直想错了！”

sentences.en: And that's when you started to get seven different kinds of vinegar, and 14 different kinds of mustard, and 71 different kinds of olive oil.
sentences.zh: 从那时起，您开始获得 7 种不同的醋、14 种不同的芥末和 71 种不同的橄榄油。

sentences.en: And then eventually even Ragù hired Howard, and Howard did the exact same thing for Ragù that he did for Prego.
sentences.zh: 最终，甚至拉古也雇佣了霍华德，而霍华德为拉古做了和为普雷戈做的一模一样的事情。

sentences.en: And today, if you go to a really good supermarket, do you know how many Ragùs there are?
sentences.zh: 今天，如果你去一家非常好的超市，你知道那里有多少拉古斯吗？

sentences.en: 36! In six varieties: Cheese, Light, Robusto, Rich & Hearty, Old World Traditional -- Extra-Chunky Garden.
sentences.zh: 36！有六个品种：奶酪、清淡奶酪、罗布斯托奶酪、浓郁丰盛奶酪、旧世界传统奶酪 - Extra-Chunky Garden。

sentences.en: (Laughter) That's Howard's doing. That is Howard's gift to the American people.
sentences.zh: （笑声） 那是霍华德做的。这是霍华德送给美国人民的礼物。

sentences.en: Now why is that important? (Laughter) It is, in fact, enormously important.
sentences.zh: 为什么这很重要？ （笑声） 事实上，这非常重要。

sentences.en: I'll explain to you why. What Howard did is he fundamentally changed the way the food industry thinks about making you happy.
sentences.zh: 我会向你解释原因。霍华德所做的是从根本上改变了食品行业关于让你快乐的想法。

sentences.en: Assumption number one in the food industry used to be that the way to find out what people want to eat, what will make people happy, is to ask them.
sentences.zh: 食品行业的第一个假设曾经是，了解人们想吃什么、什么会让人们快乐的方法就是询问他们。

sentences.en: And for years and years and years, Ragù and Prego would have focus groups, and they would sit you down, and they would say, "What do you want in a spaghetti sauce?
sentences.zh: 多年来，Ragù 和 Prego 都会设立焦点小组，他们会让你坐下来，然后说：“你想要意大利面酱里的什么？

sentences.en: Tell us what you want in a spaghetti sauce."
sentences.zh: 告诉我们你想要什么意大利面酱。”

sentences.en: And for all those years -- 20, 30 years -- through all those focus group sessions, no one ever said they wanted extra-chunky.
sentences.zh: 多年来——20、30 年——通过所有这些焦点小组会议，没有人说过他们想要额外的内容。

sentences.en: Even though at least a third of them, deep in their hearts, actually did.
sentences.zh: 尽管至少有三分之一的人，在内心深处，确实这么做了。

sentences.en: (Laughter) People don't know what they want!
sentences.zh: （笑声）人们不知道自己想要什么！

sentences.en: As Howard loves to say, "The mind knows not what the tongue wants."
sentences.zh: 正如霍华德喜欢说的：“头脑不知道舌头想要什么。”

sentences.en: It's a mystery! (Laughter) And a critically important step in understanding our own desires and tastes is to realize that we cannot always explain what we want, deep down.
sentences.zh: 这是一个谜！ （笑声）理解我们自己的欲望和品味的一个至关重要的步骤是认识到我们不能总是解释我们内心深处想要什么。

sentences.en: If I asked all of you, for example, in this room, what you want in a coffee, you know what you'd say?
sentences.zh: 例如，如果我在这个房间里问你们想要喝什么咖啡，你们知道你们会说什么吗？

sentences.en: Every one of you would say, "I want a dark, rich, hearty roast."
sentences.zh: 你们每个人都会说：“我想要一种深色、浓郁、丰盛的烘焙。”

sentences.en: It's what people always say when you ask them.
sentences.zh: 当你问他们时，人们总是这么说。

sentences.en: "What do you like?" "Dark, rich, hearty roast!"
sentences.zh: “你喜欢什么？” “深色、浓郁、丰盛的烤肉！”

sentences.en: What percentage of you actually like a dark, rich, hearty roast?
sentences.zh: 有多少人真正喜欢深色、浓郁、丰盛的烘焙咖啡？

sentences.en: According to Howard, somewhere between 25 and 27 percent of you.
sentences.zh: 根据霍华德的说法，这个比例在 25% 到 27% 之间。

sentences.en: Most of you like milky, weak coffee. (Laughter) But you will never, ever say to someone who asks you what you want that "I want a milky, weak coffee."
sentences.zh: 大多数人都喜欢奶味淡的咖啡。 （笑声）但是你永远不会对问你想要什么的人说“我想要一杯奶味淡的咖啡”。

sentences.en: So that's number one thing that Howard did.
sentences.zh: 这是霍华德做的第一件事。

sentences.en: Number two thing that Howard did is he made us realize -- it's another very critical point -- he made us realize the importance of what he likes to call "horizontal segmentation."
sentences.zh: 霍华德所做的第二件事是他让我们意识到——这是另一个非常关键的一点——他让我们意识到他喜欢所说的“水平分割”的重要性。

sentences.en: Why is this critical? Because this is the way the food industry thought before Howard.
sentences.zh: 为什么这很关键？因为这是霍华德之前食品行业的思维方式。

sentences.en: What were they obsessed with in the early 80s?
sentences.zh: 80年代初他们痴迷的是什么？

sentences.en: They were obsessed with mustard. In particular, they were obsessed with the story of Grey Poupon.
sentences.zh: 他们对芥末很着迷。他们尤其着迷于格雷·波彭的故事。

sentences.en: Used to be, there were two mustards: French's and Gulden's.
sentences.zh: 过去，有两种芥末：法国芥末和古尔登芥末。

sentences.en: What were they? Yellow mustard. What's in it?
sentences.zh: 他们是什么？黄芥末。里面有什么？

sentences.en: Yellow mustard seeds, turmeric, and paprika.
sentences.zh: 黄芥末籽、姜黄和辣椒粉。

sentences.en: That was mustard. Grey Poupon came along, with a Dijon.
sentences.zh: 那是芥末。格雷·普彭（Grey Poupon）带着一辆第戎车过来了。

sentences.en: Right? Much more volatile brown mustard seed, some white wine, a nose hit, much more delicate aromatics.
sentences.zh: 正确的？棕色芥末籽的挥发性更强，一些白葡萄酒，扑鼻而来，更细腻的芳香。

sentences.en: And what do they do? They put it in a little tiny glass jar, with a wonderful enameled label on it, made it look French, even though it's made in Oxnard, California.
sentences.zh: 他们做什么？他们把它放在一个小玻璃罐里，上面贴着精美的珐琅标签，让它看起来像法国的，尽管它是在加利福尼亚州奥克斯纳德制造的。

sentences.en: (Laughter) And instead of charging a dollar fifty for the eight-ounce bottle, the way that French's and Gulden's did, they decided to charge four dollars.
sentences.zh: （笑声） 他们没有像 French's 和 Gulden's 那样对八盎司一瓶收取 50 美元，而是决定收取 4 美元。

sentences.en: And they had those ads. With the guy in the Rolls Royce, eating the Grey Poupon.
sentences.zh: 他们有那些广告。和那个开着劳斯莱斯的家伙一起吃灰色优惠券。

sentences.en: Another pulls up, and says, "Do you have any Grey Poupon?"
sentences.zh: 另一个人停下来说：“你有灰色优惠券吗？”

sentences.en: And the whole thing, after they did that, Grey Poupon takes off!
sentences.zh: 整个事情，在他们这样做之后，格雷·波彭起飞了！

sentences.en: Takes over the mustard business! And everyone's take-home lesson from that was that the way to make people happy is to give them something that is more expensive, something to aspire to.
sentences.zh: 接管芥末生意！每个人从中得到的教训是，让人们快乐的方法就是给他们一些更昂贵的东西，一些值得他们渴望的东西。

sentences.en: It's to make them turn their back on what they think they like now, and reach out for something higher up the mustard hierarchy.
sentences.zh: 这是为了让他们放弃他们现在认为自己喜欢的东西，并寻求芥末等级更高的东西。

sentences.en: (Laughter) A better mustard! A more expensive mustard!
sentences.zh: （笑声）更好的芥末！更贵的芥末！

sentences.en: A mustard of more sophistication and culture and meaning.
sentences.zh: 一种更精致、更文化、更有意义的芥末。

sentences.en: And Howard looked to that and said, "That's wrong!"
sentences.zh: 霍华德看了一眼，说道：“那是错误的！”

sentences.en: Mustard does not exist on a hierarchy. Mustard exists, just like tomato sauce, on a horizontal plane.
sentences.zh: 芥末不存在等级制度。芥末就像番茄酱一样，存在于水平面上。

sentences.en: There is no good mustard or bad mustard.
sentences.zh: 芥末没有好坏之分。

sentences.en: There is no perfect mustard or imperfect mustard.
There are only different kinds of mustards that suit different kinds of people.
He fundamentally democratized the way we think about taste.
And for that, as well, we owe Howard Moskowitz a huge vote of thanks.
Third thing that Howard did, and perhaps the most important, is Howard confronted the notion of the Platonic dish.
(Laughter) What do I mean by that? (Laughter) For the longest time in the food industry, there was a sense that there was one way, a perfect way, to make a dish.
You go to Chez Panisse, they give you the red-tail sashimi with roasted pumpkin seeds in a something reduction.
They don't give you five options on the reduction.
They don't say, "Do you want the extra-chunky reduction, or ...?"
No! You just get the reduction. Why? Because the chef at Chez Panisse has a Platonic notion about red-tail sashimi.
"This is the way it ought to be." And she serves it that way time and time again, and if you quarrel with her, she will say, "You know what? You're wrong!
This is the best way it ought to be in this restaurant."
Now that same idea fueled the commercial food industry as well.
They had a Platonic notion of what tomato sauce was.
And where did that come from? It came from Italy.
Italian tomato sauce is what? It's blended; it's thin.

The culture of tomato sauce was thin. When we talked about "authentic tomato sauce" in the 1970s, we talked about Italian tomato sauce, we talked about the earliest Ragùs, which had no visible solids, right?
Which were thin, you just put a little bit and it sunk down to the bottom of the pasta.
That's what it was. And why were we attached to that?
Because we thought that what it took to make people happy was to provide them with the most culturally authentic tomato sauce, A.
And B, we thought that if we gave them the culturally authentic tomato sauce, then they would embrace it.
And that's what would please the maximum number of people.
In other words, people in the cooking world were looking for cooking universals.
They were looking for one way to treat all of us.
And it's good reason for them to be obsessed with the idea of universals, because all of science, through the 19th century and much of the 20th, was obsessed with universals.
Psychologists, medical scientists, economists were all interested in finding out the rules that govern the way all of us behave.
But that changed, right? What is the great revolution in science of the last 10, 15 years?
It is the movement from the search for universals to the understanding of variability.
Now in medical science, we don't want to know, necessarily, just how cancer works, we want to know how your cancer is different from my cancer.
I guess my cancer different from your cancer.
Genetics has opened the door to the study of human variability.
What Howard Moskowitz was doing was saying, "This same revolution needs to happen in the world of tomato sauce."
And for that, we owe him a great vote of thanks.
I'll give you one last illustration of variability, and that is -- oh, I'm sorry.

Howard not only believed that, but he took it a second step, which was to say that when we pursue universal principles in food, we aren't just making an error; we are actually doing ourselves a massive disservice.
And the example he used was coffee. And coffee is something he did a lot of work with, with Nescafé.

If I were to ask all of you to try and come up with a brand of coffee -- a type of coffee, a brew -- that made all of you happy, and then I asked you to rate that coffee, the average score in this room for coffee would be about 60 on a scale of 0 to 100.

If, however, you allowed me to break you into coffee clusters, maybe three or four coffee clusters, and I could make coffee just for each of those individual clusters, your scores would go from 60 to 75 or 78.
The difference between coffee at 60 and coffee at 78 is a difference between coffee that makes you wince, and coffee that makes you deliriously happy.
That is the final, and I think most beautiful lesson, of Howard Moskowitz: that in embracing the diversity of human beings, we will find a surer way to true happiness.
Thank you. (Applause)
sentences.zh: 谢谢。 （掌声）
